opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the honest answer is that nobody knows the exact number. But I think we're asking the question slightly wrong if we think about it as one fixed number we have to hit before anything works.

The way I think about it is that there are really two phases. The first is getting to the point where robots are good enough to be useful in the real world, maybe not perfect, but useful enough that people actually want to deploy them. The second phase is what happens after that, where the robots are out there doing real work and every hour of deployment produces more data. That second phase is where the scaling really kicks in, because the data collection stops being a cost center and becomes a byproduct of doing something valuable.

So the question I care about most is how much data you need to get across that first threshold. There, I think we're actually a lot closer than people might assume. A big part of it is that we're not starting from scratch anymore. We can build on vision-language models that have already absorbed a huge amount of knowledge from the web: what objects are, how the world is organized, what people mean when they ask for something. The robot data doesn't have to teach the model all of that. It has to teach the model how to connect that knowledge to physical action. That's a much narrower problem, though still a hard one.

The other thing we've seen is that diversity matters a lot more than raw volume. If you collect a million demonstrations of folding the same shirt on the same table, you get a really good shirt-folding robot on that table and not much else. If you collect data across many different robots, homes, objects, and tasks, you start to see real generalization, where the model can handle situations it never saw because it has learned something more general about manipulation. So when people ask how much data you need, I'd say the more useful question is how much variety you need, and how you set things up so the variety keeps growing.

And I think autonomous improvement is the piece that ultimately makes this tractable. Human demonstrations get you started, but they're expensive and they don't scale forever. Eventually the robot has to learn from its own experience, from its mistakes, from corrections, from reinforcement learning on real-world interaction. Once that loop is working, you're not limited by how many people you can pay to teleoperate. You're limited by how many robots are out there doing things.

So my rough picture is that we need enough diverse data to get to a flywheel, not enough data to solve robotics outright. I think that's a much more achievable target, and probably one we can hit within a few years rather than decades.

r001.rationale: It says the goal is enough diverse data to reach a self-sustaining flywheel, rather than enough data to solve robotics outright.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we don't know the exact number, but we have a pretty good sense of the shape of the problem. And the shape of the problem is actually encouraging, because we've seen this movie before in other domains.

If you look at language models, or vision models, nobody sat down beforehand and said "okay, we need exactly this many tokens." What happened is that people found a recipe that scaled, and then as you poured more data into it, it kept getting better in a predictable way. And once you have that predictability, the question of "how much data do you need" becomes a question of "how good do you want it to be," which is a much more tractable question. So what I care about most is not the absolute number, it's whether we're on that kind of curve. And I think in the last couple of years we've started to see evidence that we are.

Now, the thing that makes robotics different is where the data comes from. For language, the data was just sitting there on the internet. For robots, you have to go out and collect it. The robot has to actually do things in the world. And that's slow and expensive, so people get very worried about it. But I'd push back a bit on the pessimism there, for a couple of reasons.

One is that robots can collect their own data. That's kind of the whole point. A language model can't go generate more internet, but a robot that's deployed and doing useful work is producing experience every second it's operating. So if you can get to the point where the robot is good enough to be deployed somewhere, even in a narrow setting, you've turned the data problem from a fixed cost into something that compounds. That flywheel is the thing I'm most excited about.

The second reason is that the pretraining we get from other modalities does a lot of the heavy lifting. A lot of what a robot needs to know is not really about motor control. It's about what objects are, how the world is organized, what a person means when they say "put the dishes away." Those things you can get from vision and language data that already exists in enormous quantities. So the robot-specific data doesn't have to teach the model everything from scratch. It has to teach the model the part that's actually specific to embodiment, which is how to turn all that understanding into physical action. And that's a smaller slice than people sometimes assume.

So if you want a rough intuition: I think we need orders of magnitude more robot data than we have now, but I don't think we need orders of magnitude more than is achievable. The gap is closable with the kinds of deployments that are starting to happen. And I'd say the bottleneck I worry about more than raw quantity is diversity. A million hours of a robot doing the same task in the same lab is worth a lot less than a hundred thousand hours spread across many environments, many objects, many embodiments. Breadth is what gives you generalization, and generalization is what we actually need.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot deployed in a narrow setting can collect experience and start a compounding flywheel. But it does not propose measuring data needs by the amount needed to reach that point, as opposed to the amount needed to solve robotics fully.

astra-6.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don’t know yet. And part of the difficulty is that the amount of data you need depends enormously on what you can bring in from other sources. If your robot has to learn everything about the world from its own experience, that’s a very different proposition from a robot that can build on what a model has already learned from images, videos, and language.

There’s a lot about the world that you can learn without having a robot body. You can learn what objects are, what people tend to do with them, and what a successful outcome looks like. But there are also things that are much harder to learn just by watching. How much force should you apply? What do you do when something slips? Those are things where interaction really matters.

So I would frame the question as: how much robot experience do we need to connect all that other knowledge to action? And then, can we get a process going where the robots themselves collect the experience that makes them better?

If all the data has to come from people remotely operating robots, you can scale that up, but every additional hour requires somebody’s time. If the robot can attempt tasks, recognize when it succeeds, and learn from those attempts, then you have a much more scalable process. Of course, getting that process to work reliably is itself a substantial research problem.

The milestone I’d look for isn’t a particular number of hours. It’s whether adding more diverse experience produces predictable improvements, including on tasks and in environments that weren’t in the training data. Once you have that, you can start making meaningful estimates about how much more data you need. Before that, a number can sound precise without actually telling you very much.

r001.rationale: It frames the key question as how much robot experience is needed to connect existing knowledge to action and start a process where robots collect experience that improves them. It identifies predictable gains from more experience as the milestone, rather than a fixed amount needed to solve robotics outright.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don’t know yet. And part of the reason we don’t know is that the amount of data you need depends enormously on what kind of generalization you’re asking for.

If you want a robot to do one particular task in one particular setting, we know how to do that with relatively little data. But that’s a very different proposition from a robot that you can put into somebody’s home, tell it what to do, and expect it to handle objects and situations it hasn’t encountered before.

The thing I’m most interested in is whether we can get into a regime where each new task doesn’t require its own separate data collection effort. You collect experience across many tasks, many environments, many robots, and learning one thing makes the robot better at learning other things. Then the relevant question becomes less, ‘How many demonstrations do I need for this task?’ and more, ‘How much experience does the whole system need before it can acquire a new skill efficiently?’

There’s also a distinction between data that has to come from a robot and data that can come from elsewhere. Video can teach you a lot about what happens in the world, what objects are, what successful behavior looks like. But it doesn’t directly tell you what motor commands to issue or how something will feel when you touch it. So I would expect a combination: broad knowledge from other sources, grounded by actual robotic experience.

My guess is that we’ll need substantially more robot data than we have today. But I wouldn’t take the data requirements of a system trained on a narrow task and simply multiply them by the number of tasks we want. The whole point is to get transfer. Whether that transfer improves fast enough as we scale is the question we need to answer experimentally.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transfer across tasks and how much experience a system needs to learn new skills efficiently, but it does not propose measuring data needs by the amount required to start a self-sustaining data-collection flywheel.
